newsitem.title: USA: Currency seen weak link in Latin American growth.
newsitem.headline: Currency seen weak link in Latin American growth.

text.p: The stable currencies of major Latin American countries could become the Achilles heel of the region's economy, dampening growth and setting the stage for painful adjustments in the future, U.S. economists and Latin American market specialists said.

They said some currencies were overvalued, which has led to rising trade deficits and high real interest rates, but the alternative was equally unpalatable as a depreciation would threaten to rekindle inflation and reduce foreign capital inflows.

In a panel discussion on the investment climate in Latin America at the Council of the Americas on Friday, the economists carefully couched their forecasts to underscore the strength in the long-term, while pointing out potential risks.

Lawrence Krohn, managing director of Latin America Economic Research at UBS Securities, said the major Latin American countries have a "fixation on disinflation," which, he added, they are pursuing at the expense of other goals.

Traumatized by hyper-inflation, Argentina pegged the peso to the U.S. dollar, which has tamed inflation but made the Argentine economy vulnerable to the swings in U.S. interest rates, said Lawrence Goodman, head of Latin America Economic Research at Salomon Brothers Inc.
"The exchange rate is the weakest link," he said.
Goodman estimated that the Brazilian real is 15 percent overvalued, which has led to widening trade deficits.
For Venezuela, thanks to abundant oil revenues, the government could support an overvalued bolivar, but such an imbalance would be unsustainable over time, he added.

Currency strength was a source of concern because it results from overeliance on monetary policy without tackling tougher fiscal measures, such as changing government spending and tax rates, said Javier Murcio, director of Latin American economics at CS First Boston Corp.

All the panelists said they expected the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise the overnight bank lending, or federal funds, rate by another 50 basis points this year following its 25 basis point increase in March. However, any impact on the economies of Latin America was likely to be subdued.
Unlike in 1994, major Latin economies are less vulnerable to outside shocks, thanks to economic recovery and the absence of excessive leverage, they said.
Under these circumstances, the economists did not foresee any abrupt shift in the currency regimes this year.
But rising U.S. interest rates was casting a pall on the Latin debt market in the short-term, said another panel of debt strategists.

The "phobia" of higher interest rates still strikes terror in the Latin debt market even though the economies are on a sounder footing, said Martin Shubert, chairman of European InterAmerican Finance Corp.

Lawrence Brainard, managing director of Chase Securities Inc, expected another round of selling in Latin debt markets in the next six to eight weeks following the first leg down in March. But unlike the first leg of the recent selloff, the coming squall would bring Latin debt prices lower in line with U.S. Treasuries, while leaving sovereign credit spreads mostly intact, he predicted.
Joyce Chang, managing director of emerging markets fixed income research at Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, agreed with the assessment: "The market will see another leg lower before improvement," she said.
